nameStory: This shrub gets its name 'flowering almond' because of its spectacular spring blooms that resemble those of true almond trees, though it's actually more closely related to cherries and plums. The 'dwarf' part of its alternate name refers to its compact size compared to full-sized fruit trees. Despite the almond connection in its name, this plant is grown purely for ornamental beauty rather than edible nuts.
description: Flowering almond is a small, compact shrub that reaches about 5 feet tall and wide. It's a member of the rose family, closely related to cherries and plums. This ornamental plant is prized for its stunning spring flower display of white or pink blooms that cover the branches before the leaves fully emerge. Originally from China, it's planted in New England gardens as a decorative shrub.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: The showstopping feature - masses of white or pink flowers in spring, either single (5 petals) or double (many layered petals) depending on the variety. The flowers have a sweet, delicate fragrance and appear along the branches before leaves fully develop.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A neat, rounded shrub about 5 feet tall with multiple stems from the base. The branches have a slightly arching habit and feel smooth to the touch when young.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Light green, pointed leaves arranged alternately along the branches. The leaves feel thin and papery, with a smooth texture and finely toothed edges that you can feel if you run your finger along the margin.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, dark red fruits appear in summer, though they're not commonly produced on ornamental varieties. The fruits are about the size of a small cherry but are typically dry and not palatable.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young branches have smooth, reddish-brown bark that feels sleek under your fingers. Older stems develop a slightly rougher texture with shallow grooves.

habitat: In New England, flowering almond is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like home gardens, parks, and landscaped areas. It prefers sunny locations with well-draining soil and is often planted as a specimen shrub or in mixed borders. With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this ornamental shrub is quite uncommon in the region.

seasonality.spring: The star season - covered in showy white or pink flowers from April to early May, blooming before leaves fully expand. This is when the plant is most easily identified and most spectacular.
seasonality.summer: Green foliage fills out the shrub, and small dark red fruits may appear. The plant looks like a typical small-leaved shrub during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before dropping, though fall color is not particularly notable. The shrub begins to look bare as winter approaches.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's rounded growth habit. Smooth, reddish-brown twigs and small buds are visible along the stems.

funFact: Despite being called 'flowering almond,' this plant is actually more closely related to your backyard cherry tree than to the almonds in your snack mix - it's all about those showy flowers rather than tasty nuts!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other ornamental Prunus species like ornamental cherry trees, but flowering almond stays much smaller (shrub vs. tree) and has a more rounded, multi-stemmed growth habit. The compact size and masses of flowers appearing before leaves are key distinguishing features.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'almond' is misleading since this plant doesn't produce edible almonds and is grown purely for ornamental purposes. It's also sometimes called 'Chinese bush cherry' which is more accurate given its true relationships within the cherry-plum genus Prunus.
compareHints: Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental. It differs from beach plum by preferring garden settings over coastal areas, and from black cherry by its small stature and extremely showy spring flower display that appears before the leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
